title: Does Water Help a Hangover? What It Fixes and What It Doesn't
excerpt: Water fixes the dehydration part of a hangover, but not the rest. How alcohol dehydrates you, why water between drinks and before bed helps, how much to drink, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does water help a hangover? It fixes dehydration, not the rest. Why water between drinks and before bed helps, how much to drink, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** water helps a hangover, but it fixes only one piece of it. Alcohol makes your body lose more fluid than you take in, and that dehydration explains the thirst, the dry mouth, the lightheaded feeling when you stand up, and part of the headache. Water fixes that. What water can't fix is everything else a hangover is made of: the toxic by-products of breaking down alcohol, the inflammation it sets off, the poor sleep, and the irritated stomach. That's why someone can drink a liter of water before bed and still wake up feeling rough.

**The quick rules:** Have a glass of water with every alcoholic drink, mainly because it slows you down. Drink one or two normal glasses before bed. The next morning, sip water steadily alongside food until your urine is pale yellow. Don't chug huge amounts at once. If you've been vomiting or had diarrhea, switch to an oral rehydration drink rather than plain water. And if you can't keep any fluids down, read the "when to see a doctor" box below.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research for adults who drink socially. **See a doctor or get urgent care if** you can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, you have vomited repeatedly or see blood in your vomit, you haven't passed urine in eight hours or more, you feel faint or confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish or very pale skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it is not something to sleep off. Separately, if you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you stop or cut down, that may be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so tell a doctor plainly what you've been drinking.

## Does Water Help a Hangover? What It Fixes and What It Doesn't

A hangover isn't one problem. It's a bundle of several things happening at once, and dehydration is only one of them. Researchers who study hangovers, including the international Alcohol Hangover Research Group, generally describe it as a mix of:

- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol makes you urinate more than you drink, so you end up behind on fluid.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. It's linked to nausea, flushing, and a fast heartbeat.
- **Inflammation.** Alcohol triggers an immune response, and inflammatory signals in the blood have been tied to how bad people feel the next day.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night, so you wake up tired even after "enough" hours.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which feeds nausea and that sour, unsettled feeling.
- **Low blood sugar.** Your liver is busy with alcohol and makes less glucose, which can add shakiness and weakness, especially if you didn't eat.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more of these by-products of fermentation and aging, and they may make hangovers worse for some people.

Water directly addresses the first item on that list. It can indirectly help a little with the headache and the dizziness that come from low fluid. It has no real effect on acetaldehyde, inflammation, broken sleep, or congeners.

That matters because one of the more surprising findings in hangover research is that **dehydration and hangover severity don't line up as neatly as most people assume.** Studies that measured hydration markers and hormone levels in hungover volunteers have generally found that these markers don't closely predict how bad someone feels. One survey study led by researchers at Utrecht University (van de Loo and colleagues, 2020) compared drinkers who reported drinking water alongside alcohol with those who didn't. The water drinkers reported less thirst and dry mouth the next day, but their overall hangover severity wasn't meaningfully lower.

So the realistic expectation is this: water makes the *thirsty, dry, dizzy* part of a hangover better. It is worth doing, it's free, and it carries almost no risk. It just isn't a cure.

## Why Alcohol Dehydrates You in the First Place

Most people know alcohol makes you pee more. Here's why.

Your brain releases a hormone called **vasopressin** (also called antidiuretic hormone). Its job is to tell your kidneys to hold on to water rather than send it to your bladder. Alcohol lowers vasopressin. With less of that "hold on to water" signal, your kidneys let more water go.

A classic experiment from the 1940s (Eggleton, published in the *Journal of Physiology* in 1942) found that alcohol increased urine output in proportion to the amount consumed, and that figure is still the one textbooks quote. Two details from later research are worth knowing:

1. **The effect is strongest while your blood alcohol is rising.** Once you stop drinking and your blood alcohol plateaus or falls, the extra urine production tends to fade. That's why you can be racing to the bathroom early in the night and then wake up very dry, with no more extra urine to show for it.
2. **Stronger drinks matter more.** Studies from Loughborough University (Hobson and Maughan, 2010) and later work on beer of different strengths have found that low-strength drinks produce little or no net fluid loss, while stronger drinks do. A weak beer brings a lot of water along with its alcohol. A shot of liquor brings almost none.

Other things pile on during a night out: salty snacks, dancing in a warm room, sweating, and sleeping in dry air for eight hours without drinking anything. Some people also vomit or get diarrhea, which causes much bigger fluid and salt losses than alcohol's effect on the kidneys. If that's you, plain water alone isn't the best fix (more on that below).

## Water Between Drinks: The Most Useful Habit, for a Different Reason

"Have a glass of water between drinks" is one of the most common pieces of hangover advice. It's good advice, but probably not for the reason people think.

The biggest predictor of how bad a hangover will be is simply **how much alcohol you drink**, and how fast. Anything that lowers the total amount tends to help. Alternating each drink with a glass of water does exactly that:

- **It slows your pace.** A glass of water between drinks roughly doubles the time between alcoholic ones, so you drink less over the same evening.
- **It fills you up.** You're less likely to order another round on autopilot when you aren't thirsty.
- **It keeps your blood alcohol lower.** A slower pace gives your liver more time to keep up, since it can only clear roughly one standard drink an hour.
- **It does offset some fluid loss**, which helps with thirst and dry mouth the next day.

There is no good evidence that water between drinks *prevents* a hangover if you still drink the same amount of alcohol. But because it nearly always means drinking less, it's one of the most effective habits you can adopt. A few ways to make it stick:

- Order water at the same time as every drink, so it's already in front of you.
- Use sparkling water with lime if plain water feels like a chore at a bar. It looks like a drink, which helps if you'd rather not field questions.
- Drink the water first, then the alcoholic drink.
- If you're hosting, put a jug of water on the table where people can see it.

For more habits that genuinely lower your chances of a bad morning, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) ranks them by how good the evidence is.

## Water Before Bed: Worth It, Within Reason

Drinking water before bed is a sensible move. You usually go to sleep already behind on fluid, and then you go seven or eight hours without drinking anything. Topping up before you sleep means you wake up less parched.

A few practical tips:

- **One or two normal glasses is plenty.** Forcing down a liter right before sleep mostly means getting up to use the bathroom at 4 a.m., and alcohol already breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Poor sleep is a big part of why hangovers feel so bad, so you don't want to make it worse.
- **Put a full glass or bottle by the bed.** Waking up thirsty in the night and having water within reach is often more useful than a big glass just before lights out.
- **Eat something small if you can.** Water with a bit of food, especially something with a little salt, is absorbed and kept better than water on an empty stomach. Toast, crackers, or a banana all work.
- **Skip the extra alcohol "nightcap."** It adds to the fluid loss and the sleep disruption.

If you regularly wake at 3 or 4 a.m. after drinking and can't get back to sleep, that's a separate problem from dehydration. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what alcohol does to the second half of the night.

## How Much Water Should You Drink for a Hangover?

There isn't a single right number, because it depends on how much you drank, how much you sweated, your size, and whether you vomited. These rough guides work for most people:

| When | What to aim for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| While drinking | About one glass of water per alcoholic drink | Slows your pace and offsets some fluid loss |
| Before bed | One or two normal glasses, plus water by the bed | You'll go hours without fluid |
| Next morning | Steady sips over a few hours, with food | Gradual drinking is kept better than gulping |
| Signal you're caught up | Pale yellow urine and thirst gone | A simple, reliable at-home check |

The most useful check is the color of your urine. Dark yellow means you're still behind. Pale straw-colored means you're in good shape. Completely clear and very frequent means you can ease off. (Some B-vitamin supplements turn urine bright yellow regardless, so keep that in mind if you take them.)

### Can you drink too much water?

It's uncommon, but yes. Drinking a very large amount of plain water in a short period, especially after heavy sweating or vomiting, can dilute the sodium in your blood. Doctors call this hyponatremia. The early signs (headache, nausea, fatigue, confusion) look a lot like a hangover, which makes it easy to miss. People sometimes make this worse by thinking "I still feel bad, so I need more water" and drinking several liters in an hour.

The fix is simple: **sip steadily over hours rather than chugging**, eat something with a little salt, and if you've lost a lot of fluid through vomiting or diarrhea, use an oral rehydration solution instead of plain water. If confusion, a severe headache, or vomiting gets worse rather than better, get medical help.

## Water vs Electrolyte Drinks vs Everything Else

Plain water isn't your only option. Here's how the common choices compare for a typical hangover:

| Drink | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Plain water** | Everyday hangover thirst, especially with food | Doesn't replace salts after vomiting or diarrhea |
| **Oral rehydration solution** (like Pedialyte) | Vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, or no appetite | Costs more; overkill for a mild hangover |
| **Sports drinks** (like Gatorade) | Easy to drink, some sugar if you can't eat | Usually more sugar and less sodium than rehydration solutions |
| **Coconut water** | A pleasant alternative with potassium | Fairly low in sodium; not a medical rehydration drink |
| **Broth or soup** | Fluid, salt, and something gentle to eat | Can be very salty; check the label |
| **Coffee or tea** | Caffeine-withdrawal headache in regular drinkers | Can irritate the stomach; drink water too |
| **More alcohol ("hair of the dog")** | Nothing useful | Just delays the hangover and adds more fluid loss |

The reason oral rehydration solutions work better than plain water when you've lost a lot of fluid is that they contain a specific balance of sodium and glucose. Your gut absorbs sodium and glucose together, and water follows them in. That's the same principle behind the World Health Organization's oral rehydration formula used for diarrhea illness. For an ordinary hangover where you've just been drinking and urinating, though, water plus breakfast gives you the same salts more cheaply.

It's also worth repeating the research point from earlier: blood levels of electrolytes like sodium and potassium haven't been found to track closely with how bad a hangover feels. Electrolyte drinks can help you rehydrate faster, but they're not a hangover cure either.

If you want to go deeper on the options, see our comparisons of [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover), [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover), and whether to take [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking). Our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) covers the rest.

## Does Water Cure a Hangover? Common Myths

A few beliefs about water and hangovers are worth clearing up.

**Myth: "If I drink enough water, I won't get a hangover."** There is no good evidence that water alone prevents a hangover. It helps with the dehydration part. If you drink enough alcohol to get a bad hangover, water will make it somewhat less miserable, not absent.

**Myth: "Water flushes alcohol out of your system faster."** Almost all alcohol is broken down by your liver at a fairly steady rate. Only a small fraction leaves through urine, breath, and sweat. Drinking water won't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it won't sober you up. Only time does that.

**Myth: "A hangover is basically just dehydration."** Dehydration is one ingredient. Acetaldehyde, inflammation, poor sleep, and stomach irritation are just as important, which is why people who stay well hydrated can still get bad hangovers.

**Myth: "Hangover headaches are always from dehydration."** Some of it is. But alcohol also affects blood vessels and inflammatory signals in ways that can cause headaches even when you're well hydrated. Our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers what helps beyond water.

**Myth: "IV drips are the real cure."** IV hydration clinics deliver fluid directly into a vein, which does rehydrate you quickly. For someone who can keep fluids down, drinking water and an oral rehydration drink achieves much the same for a tiny fraction of the cost. IV fluids make clear medical sense when someone can't keep anything down, and in that situation a proper urgent care visit is a better bet than a wellness clinic.

## A Simple Hydration Plan for a Night Out

Putting it all together, here's a plan that doesn't take any effort to remember.

**Before you go out**
- Eat a real meal with some protein, fat, and carbohydrates. Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption.
- Drink a glass of water so you don't start the night thirsty (thirst makes the first drink go down fast).

**While you're drinking**
- One glass of water with every alcoholic drink.
- Favor lower-strength drinks if you can, and avoid rounds of shots.
- Keep a rough count. The single biggest factor in tomorrow's hangover is how many drinks you have tonight.

**Before bed**
- One or two normal glasses of water and a small snack.
- Put water by the bed.
- If you've vomited, sip a rehydration drink instead of plain water.

**The next morning**
- Start with a glass of water, then eat something gentle.
- Keep sipping through the morning until your urine is pale and the thirst is gone.
- If your stomach is unsettled, take small sips every few minutes rather than big gulps. Our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more on settling your stomach.
- Rest. Most hangovers ease within a day; our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains the usual timeline.

## When Water Isn't Enough: When to See a Doctor

For a typical hangover, water, food, and rest are all you need. But there are times when the problem is more than a hangover, and drinking more water at home isn't the right answer.

> **Get medical care if you:**
> - Can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, or keep vomiting
> - See blood in your vomit or have black, tarry stools
> - Haven't urinated in eight hours or more, or your urine is very dark
> - Feel faint when you stand, or actually pass out
> - Feel confused, very drowsy, or not like yourself
> - Have a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest
> - Have severe stomach pain, especially pain that spreads to your back
>
> **Call 911 or your local emergency number** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Don't leave them to sleep it off, and don't try to make them drink water if they're very drowsy, because they could choke. Lay them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.
>
> **About withdrawal:** if you drink heavily most days and notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you stop or cut back, that may be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become serious, so tell a doctor honestly how much you've been drinking. They can help you cut down safely.

## Where DHM Fits In

Water handles the dehydration part of a hangover. It doesn't touch the alcohol-processing side, which is where most hangover supplements, including DHM, aim.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, which have suggested effects on alcohol metabolism and on the liver. Human data is much more limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers outright. It also doesn't replace water, food, or simply drinking less. Some people find it a useful addition to the basics.

If you'd like to try it alongside good hydration habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and if you take any regular medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

Water helps a hangover by fixing dehydration, which is real but only one part of why you feel bad. The most valuable water habit is a glass between drinks, mainly because it makes you drink less alcohol. A glass or two before bed and steady sipping the next morning will ease thirst, dry mouth, and dizziness. If you've been vomiting, switch to an oral rehydration drink. And if you can't keep fluids down or something feels seriously wrong, get medical help rather than trying to drink your way through it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does drinking water help a hangover?**

Yes, but only partly. Water fixes the dehydration part of a hangover, which helps with thirst, dry mouth, dizziness on standing, and some of the headache. It does nothing about the other causes, such as the toxic by-product acetaldehyde, the inflammation alcohol triggers, poor sleep, and an irritated stomach. Expect water to take the edge off, not to make a bad hangover disappear.

**Should I drink water before bed after drinking alcohol?**

Yes. A glass or two of water before bed is one of the easiest helpful habits. Alcohol makes you pass more urine than you take in, so you often go to bed already behind on fluid. Topping up before sleep means you wake up less dry. Keep it to a normal glass or two rather than forcing down a large amount, which mostly means more trips to the bathroom and worse sleep.

**Does drinking water between alcoholic drinks prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that it prevents a hangover on its own. Its biggest benefit is indirect: a glass of water between drinks slows you down, so you end up drinking less alcohol, and the amount of alcohol is what drives hangover severity most. Studies of drinkers suggest water during the night reduces thirst and dry mouth the next day, but it does not reliably reduce overall hangover severity.

**How much water should I drink for a hangover?**

There is no exact number. A practical approach is one glass of water for each alcoholic drink during the night, a glass or two before bed, and then steady sipping the next morning until your urine is pale yellow. Spread it out. Drinking several liters very quickly is not more helpful and can be harmful in rare cases because it dilutes the sodium in your blood.

**Is water or an electrolyte drink better for a hangover?**

For a typical hangover, plain water plus some food is enough, because food replaces salts naturally. An electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution makes more sense if you have been vomiting, had diarrhea, sweated a lot dancing or in the heat, or can't face food. Research has not found that electrolyte levels in the blood track closely with how bad a hangover feels, so electrolytes are a helper, not a cure.

**Why am I so thirsty after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol lowers the level of vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, your kidneys release more urine than usual while your blood alcohol is rising. Salty bar food, sweating, and a dry room overnight add to it. The result is that you wake up short on fluid and your body signals that with strong thirst and a dry mouth.

**Can you drink too much water with a hangover?**

It's uncommon, but yes. Drinking a very large amount of plain water in a short time, especially after heavy sweating or vomiting, can lower the sodium level in your blood. Early signs include headache, nausea, and confusion, which are easy to confuse with a hangover. Sip steadily over hours instead of chugging, eat something salty, and seek medical help if confusion, severe headache, or vomiting gets worse rather than better.

**Does coffee count toward hydration when hungover?**

Mostly yes. A regular cup or two of coffee adds fluid overall for people who drink it often, because the mild water-losing effect of caffeine is smaller than the water in the cup. Coffee can help a caffeine-withdrawal headache if you normally drink it. It can also upset an already irritated stomach, so drink water alongside it and don't rely on coffee as your only fluid.
